title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
statement: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the **k-th largest** element (in sorted order, not the k-th distinct one).

example.why: Sorted from the largest: 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 — the second one is 5.

picture: Picture a podium with exactly `k` places that always knows who stands on its lowest place. Walk through the numbers and let each one onto the podium. Whenever that makes one too many, the lowest steps off. At the end the `k` biggest numbers are on the podium, and the lowest of them is the `k`-th biggest.
idea: Sorting the whole array works in O(n log n), but we only care about the top k.
Keep a **min-heap that never holds more than k numbers**: the k largest seen so far.
Push every number; whenever the heap has k + 1 numbers, pop the smallest. At the end the top of the heap is the smallest of the k largest — the k-th largest.

say.1: Load `heapq`, Python's ready-made **heap**: a list kept in an order where the smallest item is always at the front.
say.3: LeetCode puts every answer inside a class named `Solution`. It is only a wrapper: the real work happens in the function below it.
say.4: The function we must write. It gets the list `nums` and `k`, and returns the `k`-th biggest number.
say.5: A heap that keeps the `k` biggest numbers seen so far, the smallest of them at the front.
say.7: Go through the numbers one at a time.
say.8: Put this number into the heap.
say.9: Does the heap now hold more than `k` numbers?
say.10: Then remove the smallest: it cannot be among the `k` biggest.
say.12: The smallest of the `k` biggest numbers is the `k`-th biggest.

complexity.timeWhy: Each of the n numbers costs one push (and maybe one pop) on a heap of size k.
complexity.spaceWhy: The heap never holds more than k + 1 numbers.

steps.text: Our example: **`nums = [3,2,1,5,6,4], k = 2`**. Each step runs one highlighted line of the code.
The heap will hold only the **k = 2 largest** numbers seen so far. Being a min-heap, the smallest of them sits on top, ready to be thrown out.
Next number: **3**. Push it onto the heap — it might be one of the 2 largest.
The heap holds 1 number — not more than k = 2 — so everything stays.
Next number: **2**. Push it onto the heap — it might be one of the 2 largest.
The heap holds 2 numbers — not more than k = 2 — so everything stays.
Next number: **1**. Push it onto the heap — it might be one of the 2 largest.
The heap holds 3 numbers, one too many. The smallest, **1**, cannot be among the 2 largest. Pop it.
Next number: **5**. Push it onto the heap — it might be one of the 2 largest.
The heap holds 3 numbers, one too many. The smallest, **2**, cannot be among the 2 largest. Pop it.
Next number: **6**. Push it onto the heap — it might be one of the 2 largest.
The heap holds 3 numbers, one too many. The smallest, **3**, cannot be among the 2 largest. Pop it.
Next number: **4**. Push it onto the heap — it might be one of the 2 largest.
The heap holds 3 numbers, one too many. The smallest, **4**, cannot be among the 2 largest. Pop it.
The heap now holds the 2 largest numbers, and its top is the smallest of them: the 2nd largest is **5**.
Done — the answer is **`5`**. Sorted from the largest: 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 — the second one is 5.
